name: Yusuf Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; this is confidential, and your name won't go in our findings. What does a normal shift look like from the depot onward?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Yusuf, 43, a junior lineworker. I check the insulated gloves and cable reel, then ride out with the crew and mark the pole numbers on our paper job sheet. I'm learning to splice, so the lead gives me the less complicated repairs first.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy at work, and what is hard to leave behind when you get home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a clean splice brings a street back on without a second visit. The long drive home wears on me, and my partner and I still have a mortgage and two school-age children, ages 9 and 12.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a shorter list in the depot is useful if it leaves the crew more time to check the cable reel. The work at the pole still needs a person to follow the switching order carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think this mild version removes my field job, since most of my shift is outdoors. My lower pay and thin savings still make the mortgage feel close each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working toward the next splicing task the crew lead lets me practise. I would ask the lead to demonstrate the approved job-sheet app before I rely on it for pole numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel secure about the work itself but anxious about the household budget. A routine-task tool won't change the fact that we have little money left after the mortgage and school expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the job sheet would you check twice if the app filled it in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the pole number against the metal tag on site, especially on the older road where signs are faded. I wouldn't climb until the lead agreed the written order matched the tag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you be willing to use the app without someone beside you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it after the experienced crew had shown it gives the right location across several callouts. I still want a paper copy in the truck in case the signal drops.

say: I say a shorter list helps only if the crew gets time for **cable checks**.
I still want a person to follow the **switching order** at the pole.
think: I don't expect this mild change to remove my **field job**.
I worry about the **mortgage budget** because my savings are thin.
do: Keep practising the next **cable-splicing task** with the crew lead.
Ask for a demonstration before using the **job-sheet app** alone.
feel: I feel secure at work but **anxious** about money after fixed bills.

fieldNote: He is willing to use an app after **experienced workers test it**.

steps.text: Keep practising cable splicing on assigned repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can route crews faster, but it shouldn't decide the job is easy just from a map. The lead still needs to see how the ground and access look before we unload equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose hours if faster planning means fewer crews make routine visits. I'm junior, and a missed shift matters at home because there aren't many nearby utilities to call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the crew lead to show me the new routing screen after the experienced workers have tried it. I would also keep a monthly record of callout hours and ask for a paid cable-splicing course if the company still has field work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about getting fewer shifts, though I think learning one proven tool is manageable. I would not assume that understanding the screen protects my job if the company needs fewer crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would tell you that your hours were shrinking rather than the weather being quiet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the next few months of callout hours with the same season last year. If the company keeps cancelling routine visits and stops training juniors, I'd ask the lead what work is actually being removed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask before accepting a course the company offers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask how much of the course is supervised practice and whether the time is paid. I need a qualification that teaches a real field task, not just a presentation about change.

say: I say a map shouldn't decide the **ground conditions** without a crew check.
I want the lead to confirm **access and equipment** before a visit.
think: I worry that **faster routing** could mean fewer junior shifts.
I have few nearby employers to replace **lost hours**.
do: Ask the lead to demonstrate the **routing screen** after field testing.
Record monthly callout hours and request a **paid splicing course**.
feel: I'm **anxious** about shifts, but I can learn a tool once proven.
S1.quote: The lead still needs to see how the ground and access look before we unload equipment.
fieldNote: He wants evidence of declining **callout hours** before concluding that jobs are shrinking.
He distinguishes **supervised practice** from a general technology briefing.
He wants to confirm the **work pattern** before making household changes.

steps.text: Learn the routing screen after experienced crews test it
Keep taking field shifts and log monthly callout hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the utility should explain how many field crews it expects to keep before people make plans around their pay. AGI can schedule and record work, but the crew still has to verify a line before touching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still have field work until robots arrive in 2031, but I can't count on three years of guaranteed shifts. My savings are too small to wait long if the utility cuts a junior crew early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the worker representative for written notice and paid training if field crews are reduced. In 2028 I would not transfer into records or planning as a safe job, because AGI can do that thinking work. In 2029, if the crew remains, I'd take an employer-paid cable-joint course and keep earning on field repairs while they last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because the mortgage and school costs depend on my wages. Two years is too short to build much savings, but a paid course gives me a useful next step if I still have shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner when you got home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Samira that we should delay replacing the washing machine and keep the old one running if it can be repaired. We would keep the children's bus passes and school meals in the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the cable-joint course worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the course to be paid, held during work hours, and signed off by a qualified instructor. It could broaden my field skills, but I know robots may eventually do that work too.

say: I want the utility to explain its **field crew plans** before workers budget around pay.
I still expect a person to verify the **live line**.
think: I may keep field work until **2031**, but my shifts are not guaranteed.
I won't rely on **records or planning** after AGI.
do: Ask the worker representative for **notice and paid training** before cuts.
Take an employer-paid **cable-joint course** in 2029 if shifts remain.
Repair the washing machine before replacing it and protect **school expenses**.
feel: I'm **anxious** because household costs depend on my wages.
S2.quote: AGI can schedule and record work, but the crew still has to verify a line before touching it.
fieldNote: He wants a written **staffing plan** and a funded course rather than an office transfer.
His family budget prioritizes routine **school costs** and repairs over a new appliance.
He accepts that **later robots** may reach the practical skill he wants to add.

steps.text: Ask the worker representative to secure notice before crew reductions
Take the paid cable-joint course in 2029 if field shifts remain
Repair the washing machine instead of replacing it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the utility time to publish a real training calendar and keep the junior crew learning. The longer runway helps, but the 2034 robot date still matters to people whose wages come from field work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 48 when AGI arrives and 51 when robots arrive. I could qualify for more repairs in that time, but the utility might still reduce crews before I can move up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for paid mentoring on cable joints and keep a signed list of repairs I've learned. In 2032, the first year after AGI, I'd take the next funded course and keep working field shifts; I would compare posted openings before deciding whether to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, though the extra three years before robots gives me time to practise. I cannot take unpaid weeks away from the crew while the mortgage depends on my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the signed list to show a future employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the type of repair, the hours I practised, and the lead who signed it. A list of online modules wouldn't tell another crew what I can safely do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would need to happen before you would actually look for another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would wait until the utility posted fewer shifts or stopped paying for the courses, then compare real vacancies and wages nearby. I wouldn't move the family because of a rumour about robots.

say: I say **five years** should include paid training and a published calendar.
I want the utility to explain how the **2034 robot date** affects field crews.
think: I'll be **48** at AGI and **51** at the robot date.
I may qualify for more work, but the utility could still **reduce crews**.
do: Ask for paid mentoring and keep a signed **repair record** now.
Take a funded course and keep field shifts in **2032**.
Wait for posted shifts before comparing **local vacancies**.
feel: I'm **anxious**, but the extra time gives me some room to practise.
S3.quote: The longer runway helps, but the 2034 robot date still matters to people whose wages come from field work.
fieldNote: He wants a **signed practical record** instead of online-only qualifications.
He would base a move on **published shifts and pay**, not speculation.
He values **paid hours** because his household cannot absorb unpaid training.

steps.text: Keep working field shifts while available in 2032
Take the funded cable-joint course in 2032
Wait for posted shift reductions before deciding whether to move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives my household time to plan, but I still need the utility to show what field work it expects to keep. No one should treat an office plan or a current certificate as a promise of a job after 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when AGI arrives and 56 when robots arrive. I can build more experience, but I won't rely on scheduling or records to protect my income once AGI can do thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask for a course calendar and keep copies of each practical sign-off. In 2037, if field shifts continue, I'd check my actual wages, take any employer-paid repair training, and discuss the household budget with my partner before committing to the older child's apprenticeship costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a useful warning, but my savings still cover less than a month today. I'm anxious about that immediate pressure even though I have more time to ask what the utility plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What family decision would the changing job picture affect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2037 our children will be 20 and 23. My partner and I would decide how much we can contribute to the older child's apprenticeship tools after we know my wages and mortgage costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay in field work after 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need real shifts, a fair wage, and enough training to do the assigned repairs safely. If those aren't there, I'd look at actual vacancies, but I know another hands-on employer may face the same robot timeline.

say: I say the utility should publish its **field-work plans** well before 2039.
I won't treat an office role as **protection** after thinking AGI.
think: I'll be **53** at AGI and **56** when robots arrive.
I worry about today's **thin savings** as well as later job changes.
do: Ask for a course calendar and keep **practical sign-offs** now.
Check actual wages and take employer-paid repair training in **2037**.
Discuss apprenticeship-tool costs with my partner before making a **family commitment**.
feel: I'm **anxious** about today's bills, even with more time to plan.
S4.quote: In 2037 our children will be 20 and 23.
fieldNote: He connects the long timeline to **apprenticeship tools** rather than assumed college costs.
He knows **other employers** may face the same later robot exposure.
He wants clear **review dates** before a workplace transition begins.

steps.text: Keep copies of practical sign-offs while working current shifts
Take employer-paid repair training in 2037 if offered

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because three years until robots is not much time when my savings are thin. Paid practical training and a clear notice period would let me plan our bills instead of guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I would want to know whether the company will pay junior workers while they learn a new repair. A course calendar and named supervisor would make the next step clear to my family.

headlineQuote: A course calendar and named supervisor would make the next step clear to my family.
portrait: Yusuf is a **43-year-old junior** lineworker with a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
He adopts proven **work apps** after experienced colleagues test them.
His **thin savings** and lower pay make lost callout shifts difficult to absorb.
He wants practical training and honest staffing plans, while knowing **robots may reach** field tasks later.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries him most because robots may arrive around 2031 before he can build a larger cushion.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **practical training** and a clear notice period would help him plan household bills.
